title: Interview #99 Bob De Caux, Chief AI Officer at IFS
summary: Bob De Caux, Chief AI Officer at IFS, breaks down why the most dangerous moment for industrial AI comes after people start trusting it. He explains why agents still struggle when handed too much information, why guardrails against irreversible decisions matter far more than planning or memory, and why keeping live operational data out of external models is about uptime, not preference. Bob also dives into why chat will not replace the Gantt chart or the spreadsheet, how dispatchers who embraced automation still wanted an exceptions-based view to stay sharp, and the point where accountability moves from the company back to the vendor when a harness breaks. Finally, drawing on his early work modeling systems of ants, he warns that emergent failures between agents only appear at scale, and argues that LLMs will never solve forecasting and optimization on their own. title: How to Make AI-Translated Content Convert in Every Market - with Andrew Thomas of Acclaro
summary: Translating content into every language a company serves has become fast and inexpensive, but accurate translation does not ensure that content engages or converts in each market. In this episode, Andrew Thomas, Head of Marketing at Acclaro, explains why global content performance is a governance issue rather than a translation issue, and why leaders should judge localized content by the business outcome it was created to drive. He also covers testing new markets with AI-translated content before investing in local teams, building brand style guides and terminology into AI translation tools to curb shadow localization, and using automated quality checks to decide when an in-country expert needs to review content. This episode is sponsored by Acclaro AI can help you reach new markets faster, but how do you connect that investment to business results? title: Can AI Invent or Just Help Scientists Work Faster? with Richard Socher - #783
summary: AI can help scientists write code, analyze data, and draft papers. But can it generate the ideas that lead to new discoveries? Richard Socher, former chief scientist at Salesforce, founder of You.com, and co-founder of Recursive, joins us to explore the move from AI assisting researchers to AI conducting research. Starting with AI improving AI, we examine what it takes to propose ideas, run experiments, and validate results, and how those capabilities could eventually accelerate discovery across biology, chemistry, and physics. The conversation covers Recursive’s reported results in model training and GPU kernel optimization, why fast verification matters, and how reward hacking complicates the search for real improvements. We also discuss the data and experimental infrastructure needed for broader scientific discovery, whether commercial incentives can keep increasingly capable systems aligned, and Richard’s vision for a “Eureka machine.” 🗒️ Full show notes: ⁠ https://twimlai.com/go/783 .

title: How Stanford Teaches AI Coding Now
summary: What does it take to build AI agents that deliver useful, reliable work? Stanford lecturer and Monaco Head of AI Mihail Eric joins Demetrios for a conversation inside a Waymo about how AI is changing software development - and what it takes to put agents into production. Mihail explains why he rebuilt most of his Modern Software Developer course, how he teaches students to avoid shipping AI slop, and why research, planning, and verification still matter as coding agents become more capable. They discuss Claude Code, agent loops, context engineering, memory and compaction, and how to design MCP tools around what an agent needs to accomplish. Then they go inside Monaco’s approach to sales agents, from turning meetings and emails into useful insights to building a custom agent harness. Along the way: lessons from Boris and Lee Robinson’s guest lectures, why company traces are becoming valuable assets, and Monaco’s unusual approach to brand building. What’s the biggest bottleneck in your agent workflows: context, tools, or verification? Let us know in the comments. title: AI Won’t Make Our Minds Useless According to 400 Years of History
summary_html:
What if abundant intelligence makes human ambition expand rather than human relevance disappear? NLW explores Venkatesh Rao’s “Cognitive Mercantilism,” which uses the history of capitalism to challenge assumptions about AI and our intellectual future. From the agricultural revolution to today’s AI agents, the episode examines how cheaper intelligence could unlock new desires, new work, and possibilities we haven’t yet imagined.
